newsitem.title: USA: US Senate Finance chairman proposes tax cut plan.
newsitem.headline: US Senate Finance chairman proposes tax cut plan.

text.p: Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth proposed cutting taxes by $85 billion over five years with a plan that differed from legislation in the House.

Roth, a Delaware Republican, offered a bill filling in details of the tax portion of a budget agreement reached by congressional leaders and the White House last month. Similar to legislation approved by the House Ways and Means Committee last week, it included a child tax credit, higher education tax initiatives, capital gains tax reduction, estate tax relief and expanded Individual Retirement Accounts.
But it differed on some specifics. Any differences between House and Senate legislation must be worked out before tax legislation is sent to the president.
The Senate Finance Committee was to consider Roth's bill Thursday when members were to be allowed to offer amendments.
"This tax relief package is a combination of some of the best ideas from both sides of the aisle," Roth said, calling it "a bipartisan effort."

The White House has criticised the House bill and all Democrats on the Ways and Means Committee voted against it. But, without outright endorsement, Democrats and the Clinton administration spoke more favourably of the Roth bill.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the Senate tax cut proposal seemed to resolve some of the problems that were in the House version. "Roth's proposal is an improvement ... in a number of respects," Rubin said.

"The fact that we're working in a bipartisan fashion is good news," Sen. John Breaux, a Louisiana Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said. "I think the tax bill coming out of the Finance Committee will be a better product."

The biggest piece of the tax cut would be $81 billion for a $500-per-child tax credit for children under age 17. If the child is aged 13 to 16, the tax credit must be deposited in an IRA-type account earmarked for education.

As in the House legislation, Roth's bill offered a tax credit of 50 percent of up to $3,000 of college tuition. The Senate bill would also provide a credit of 75 percent of up to $2,000 for students attending community colleges and technical schools, addressing White House concerns that only doing the first part would penalise students at less-expensive schools.

Both the Roth and House bills would cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from a maximum 28 percent for individuals. But Roth's proposal would not touch the capital gains tax for corporations, while the House bill would gradually reduce it to 30 percent from 35 percent.
Married couples could exclude from taxation up to $500,000 of gain from selling a home under both proposals.

Both bills would eventually raise the threshold at which the estate tax is imposed to $1 million from the current $600,000. But Roth's bill would also immediately exclude up to $1 million from the inheritance tax for a family farm or business that comprised more than 50 percent of the estate.
Roth proposed funding for Amtrak, the rail service, at a cost of $2.3 billion over five years, paid for with a half-cent of the 4.3 cents per gallon gasoline tax.

Roth, a staunch advocate of expanding IRAs, proposed penalty-free withdrawals for first-time homebuyer expenses up to $10,000, people unemployed for a long time, and education expenses. His plan would also allow homemakers to put up to $2,000 a year in an IRA regardless of spouse participation in an employer pension plan.

The legislation would raise $53 billion over five years in tax increases and other revenue raisers, more than the $46 billion in the House bill. Revenue raisers included extension of the airline ticket tax but would reduce the tax rate to 7.5 percent from 10 percent for flights in certain rural areas.
The bill would repeal the $6 departure tax and impose a 10 percent tax on the part of the international ticket price attributable to the portion of flight in U.S. airspace.
Roth's bill would raise $6.4 billion over five years from extending the federal unemployment surtax paid by employers.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said negotiations to reconcile bills with the Senate were "always a struggle," but he believed tax cuts would ultimately be enacted. "I am very optimistic we will get a tax bill signed into law," he said.
